name: David Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, David. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the front office of a small housing association, Eastgate Homes, in a town where it's one of the bigger employers. Most of my day is booking repairs: a tenant rings about a leaking boiler, I log it, find a slot with one of our three contractors and send the letter. I also keep the tenancy files and type up the minutes for the Thursday housing meeting. I've been there just over a year, so I still check a lot of things with Margaret, who's run the office for twenty years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the work actually matters, because a broken heater in January is a real problem for a family. What wears me out is the double entry: I log a repair in the system, then again in a spreadsheet for the contractor, then again in a letter. My pay's at the bottom of the scale and Lena, my partner, is a care worker, so between us we've got maybe two weeks of money saved at any time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say good, because half the hype was always from people selling software. At the union branch meeting I'd say the real fights are still pay and staffing, not robots. Online I'd stay quiet, I don't post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my job stays roughly the same, which is fine but not great. A tool that fills in the repair letters for me would be welcome. The problem was never AI, it's that I'm on the lowest band and the rent on our flat went up again in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and try to get Margaret to show me the reporting side, because that's where the next grade is. I'd use whatever letter tool the office buys, once the others have tried it. I'd also put twenty pounds a week aside, however hard that is, because two weeks of savings is no cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved, but the old worries don't go anywhere. It's like being told the storm missed us while the roof still leaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the double entry. If a tool took that off you, what would you do with the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend more time on the phone with tenants, which is the bit I'm actually good at. Old Mr Patel on Holloway Road rings every week, and he just wants someone to listen before he tells you about his window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You and Lena have about two weeks of savings. What's the pressure you'd still carry in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent, and the fact there are only two or three offices like ours in town. If Eastgate Homes (the housing association I work for) lost a council contract, I'd have nowhere else to go without a long bus ride. So I'd still be watching the budget news closely.

say: I'd tell the union branch the **real fights** are still pay and staffing, not robots.
I'd say plainly that a lot of the **AI hype** came from people selling software.
think: Privately I think my **job stays the same**, which is fine but leaves me on the lowest pay band.
My real pressure is the **rent rise** and only two or three similar offices in town.
do: Ask Margaret to teach me the **reporting side** so I can aim for the next grade.
Use the office's **letter tool** once colleagues have tried it first.
Put **twenty pounds** a week into savings, starting this month.
feel: **Relieved** that nothing radical happens, but the old money worries stay put.
S0.quote: If Eastgate Homes (the housing association I work for) lost a council contract, I'd have nowhere else to go without a long bus ride.
fieldNote: David treats the plateau as **good news**, yet his thin cushion and few local offices keep him tense.
His **union instinct** points him at pay and staffing rather than technology.
He lights up talking about **tenants**, which hints at where he sees his own value.

steps.text: Learn the monthly repairs reporting from Margaret this winter
Use the office letter tool after colleagues trial it
Save twenty pounds a week into a separate account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a proper say in how it's brought in, not just an email from head office one Monday. I'd bring it to the union rep and ask for a meeting. With friends I'd say it's coming for the jobs people like us do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is one of the first to shrink. Logging a repair, booking a slot, writing the letter: that's exactly the list on your card. A program could book Mrs Doyle's boiler repair faster than me, and it wouldn't need a lunch break. The phone calls might stay, but there are only so many phone jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to go on any training for the new system right away, so I'm the one who knows it rather than the one it replaces. I'd join the union's working group on tech, if there is one. And I'd look at the housing officer course at the college, which is evenings, though it's three hundred pounds I don't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest, honestly. Lena's job feels safer than mine, which is strange to say when she earns less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the office would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margaret, oddly, because she's never used anything but the old system and she's two years off her pension. And Jodie, the other junior, because she's on a short contract and they'd just not renew it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push through the union. What exactly would you ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for no compulsory redundancies for two years, retraining on paid time, and that anyone moved gets kept on the same grade. Those are normal asks. Whether head office listens is another thing.

say: I'd say staff need a **proper say** in how AI comes in, not just an email.
I'd tell friends this is coming for **jobs like ours**.
think: Privately I think my **booking work** is one of the first things a program takes.
The **phone calls** might stay, but there aren't many jobs that are just phone work.
do: Sign up for **training** on the new system the week it's announced.
Join or start a **union working group** on technology at work.
Look into the evening **housing officer course**, though it costs three hundred pounds.
feel: **Tight in the chest**, and oddly aware that Lena's lower-paid job feels safer than mine.
S1.quote: A program could book Mrs Doyle's boiler repair faster than me, and it wouldn't need a lunch break.
fieldNote: David sees his tasks **listed on the card** and draws the conclusion quickly.
His first move is **collective**: union asks, no compulsory redundancies, paid retraining.
He worries about **colleagues** like Margaret and Jodie before himself.
The **course fee** of three hundred pounds is a real barrier for him.

steps.text: Volunteer for training on the new booking system straight away
Ask the union rep to start a tech working group
Apply for the evening housing officer course at the college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments have to step in fast, with something like a basic income, because nobody can retrain in two years. I'd probably share that kind of thing online, which I don't normally do. At work I think everyone would just be in shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job is gone by 2028, plain and simple. Everything I do is thinking work on a screen, so I don't get the extra three years the plumbers get. I'd be twenty-nine and out of work with no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up with the union for the campaign side straight away, because the only answer I can see is political. I'd talk to Lena about whether I should move toward care work like her, since that's hands-on and might last longer. And I'd cut everything: the streaming, the takeaway on Fridays, all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Not panicked yet, because two years is still two years, but scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says robots for hands-on work come about three years after the thinking AI. Does that matter for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It matters a lot. The contractors who fix the boilers keep working until 2031 or so, and I don't. A plumber's apprentice gets three more years than me, just because plumbing is hands-on work. It's made me think about Lena's job differently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is not long. What happens to the flat and the rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have to look at moving back near my mum, in the next town, where rent's lower. I don't want to, but on one wage that's what it would come to. I'd rather plan for that than wait for the letter.

say: I'd say government must act **fast**, maybe with a **basic income**.
I'd share that view online, which I **normally don't** do.
think: I think my **desk job is gone** by 2028.
Plumbers get **three more years** than me because their work is hands-on.
do: Join the **union campaign** for government support straight away.
Talk with Lena about moving into **care work**, which is hands-on.
Cut **streaming and takeaways** from this month.
feel: **Scared**, though not panicked, because two years is still some time.
S2.quote: A plumber's apprentice gets three more years than me, just because plumbing is hands-on work.
fieldNote: David grasps the **thinking-first** order at once and sees he gets no extra time.
He reaches for **politics and the union** as the only realistic answer.
A move toward **care work** is a new idea sparked by the robot delay.
Moving near his **mum** is a fallback he dislikes but would plan for.

steps.text: Join the union's campaign for a basic income
Ask Lena's agency about care worker training
Cancel streaming and the Friday takeaway this month
Plan a move near my mum to cut rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before really, that we need rules and support in place before it arrives. With five years I'd say there's time for a proper plan, so there's no excuse. I'd say that at the union branch and probably to our local councillor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it still ends the same way for my job, just later. Five years gives me time to get a second skill, though, and that changes things. I'd be thirty-two when it lands, which feels less hopeless than twenty-nine with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start the care certificate in the evenings, so I've got something hands-on by the time the office goes. I'd keep the office job going as long as it lasts. I'd also try to save a bit more each month, maybe forty pounds instead of twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a bit of a plan, which helps more than I expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You have five years here instead of two. What do you do in the first of those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd miss the order of it, the files and the lists. I like closing a repair ticket at four o'clock and knowing a family has hot water tonight. Care work is closer to people, which I'd like, but it's hard on your back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you went into care work like Lena, what would you miss about the office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena would laugh at me. She'd say it's not as easy as filling in forms. She's probably right, but at least it would be work a machine can't do for a few more years.

say: I'd say five years means there's **no excuse** for not planning.
I'd raise it at the union branch and with our **local councillor**.
think: I think my office job **still ends**, just later.
Five years gives me time to build a **second skill** before it lands.
do: Start the **care certificate** in the evenings during the first year.
Keep the **office job** for as long as it lasts.
Raise savings to **forty pounds** a month.
feel: **Worried**, but having a plan helps more than I expected.
S3.quote: I like closing a repair ticket at four o'clock and knowing a family has hot water tonight.
fieldNote: The **extra three years** move David from fear to a working plan.
He picks **care work** because robots reach it later, not out of love for it.
His **pride** in closing repair tickets shows what he'd lose.

steps.text: Start the evening care certificate within the first year
Write to the local councillor about support for office staff
Raise monthly savings to forty pounds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's use it: free courses, proper retraining, a plan for people like us. I'd probably be less loud about it than in the fast ones. People switch off when it's ten years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it feels almost manageable. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven, and I'd have had time to move up or out of the office. The worry is that I'd waste the time, like most people would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the housing officer course properly, maybe over two years, because that work has more judgment and visits than the booking side. I'd keep saving. And I'd keep an eye on how the office uses AI, so I'm not caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still a knot somewhere, but calmer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Does it change what you'd want from your life, not just your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me think about kids, honestly. Lena and I keep putting it off because of money. I don't want to have a baby in 2034 and lose my job in 2036. So it would shape that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still lean on the union and the government here, or more on yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. The union matters because on my own I've got no weight. But with ten years, a lot of it's on me, and I'd rather admit that than wait for someone to fix it.

say: I'd say we have a **decade**, so let's fund free courses and retraining.
I'd be **less loud** than in the fast pictures, since people switch off.
think: Privately it feels **almost manageable**, with time to move up or out.
My worry is that I'd **waste the time**, like most people.
do: Complete the **housing officer course** over two years.
Watch how the office uses **AI tools** so nothing catches me out.
feel: **Calmer**, though a knot of worry stays.
S4.quote: I don't want to have a baby in 2034 and lose my job in 2036.
fieldNote: Ten years lets David think about **family plans**, not just his job.
He admits responsibility is **partly his own**, a shift from earlier answers.
His thin savings still keep the **mood above calm**.

steps.text: Finish the housing officer course over two years
Keep the twenty pounds a week savings going
Hold off on starting a family until work is clearer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years with two weeks of savings and a desk job is the worst place to be. What would help is paid retraining on work time, and a guarantee that people like me aren't just dropped while it happens.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who aren't online much. Half our tenants don't use email. If the housing office goes fully automatic, the people who can't use a screen are the ones left waiting in the cold.

headlineQuote: If the housing office goes fully automatic, the people who can't use a screen are the ones left waiting in the cold.
portrait: David is a **27-year-old** junior office administrator who books repairs for a small housing association.
He lives with Lena, a **care worker**, on about two weeks of savings.
He's a **union** man who reaches for collective answers first.
He moves from anxious in the plateau to **alarmed** when AGI arrives in two years.
Longer warning lets him plan a **second skill**, and he eyes care or housing officer work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his desk job goes before he can save or retrain.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** on work time and a guarantee that junior staff aren't simply dropped.
